# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for quiet movies like "Perfect Days" or "Train Dreams"

**Score:** 34
**Body:** I don't know how to define this kind of movie other than quiet.

They make me feel more emotions than many other, more "emotional" movies.

If those kinds of movies are a spesific genre, I would love to know to look for more.

  
Anyway, I'm looking for more movies like these; I think what hooks me is the scope, the intimacy, the sound, and the feeling.

1. The Straight Story (1999)

Paris Texas (1985)
2. Flow. It’s animated but gave me similar vibes.
  - I set this movie up for the kids to watch thinking I'd be able to go get some chores done. 

Nope. 

I sat down with them, eyes glued to the TV, basically just in awe from start to finish. 
3. Paterson immediately comes to mind. Very quiet, intimate, and focused on the small details of an ordinary life. If Perfect Days and Train Dreams hit you emotionally, I think this one will too.

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. What is the worst historical inaccuracy you’ve seen in a movie?

**Score:** 1072
**Body:** Catch Me If You Can is an obvious one where the entire story is made up. Frank abagnale was in and out of prison the entire time he claimed to be evading the FBI. Not only that but his actual crimes were stalking women, sexual assaults and robbing middle class families and small shops.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. In *A Beatiful Mind* the central theme of it all is this heartwarming message about love triumphing over all, and how the wife stuck with him through his mental illness to the end.

In the REAL world, she divorced him over the mental illness. Even worse, he had a child with another woman prior to marrying the woman shown in the movie as his love interest. This other woman had his son. He refused to acknowledge his own son as his, and refused child support and became estranged of him. When he married a 2nd time, to the character of the film, they had a boy as well. On the divorce to his 2nd wife, he became estranged to his 2nd son as well.

In the 80s and 90s, with better meds, his mental illness improved and he has since tried to regain that relationship, and after the movie released, they actually got back together and remarried. But the key is, after the film released. The film, in the meantime, was very cleaned up to his rather messy life and terrible family relationships.
2. In recent history, that honor would go to *Gladiator II*.

Numidia-by-the-Sea, gladiators riding rhinos, and sharks in the coliseum…

Where do I begin?

Edit: I’d like to clarify that I did know the Romans had naval battles, but having *sharks* was the point which left me in disbelief.
  - It also contained a scene with a trebuchet - a technology that wouldn't exist for another thousand years.
    - Somebody is reading a newspaper in a scene.
3. Gangs of New York. In real life Bill the Butcher aka William Poole and John Morrisey are gang leaders/political figure with a fierce rivalry. Unlike the movie which shows a large scale gang war, in real life both men fought an informal bare knuckle boxing match won by Poole. Several months later associates of Morrisey shoot and kill William Poole. 
4. Catch me if you can falls under the genre of spinning a yarn. Like taking John Smith seriously. Or Chuck Barris or Marco Polo.
  - I completely agree! That's the whole point- he's conning the audience the same way he conned everyone else. Of course it's inaccurate- you're being told a story by a conman. 
5. The Greatest Showman. P.T. Barnum has the phrase "one sucker born every minute" attributed to him, and he exploited the shit out of everything within his grasp to make money off the less fortunate. He even showed off an ex-slave as an exhibit. But one healthy dose of Jackman-inspired musical washing and for some reason his public image has been successfully laundered.
6. https://preview.redd.it/tda2vgkz14kh1.jpeg?width=420&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=d05985cfbbf551a1fcdb1f0c72e421cbe72e8f22


7. Ridley Scott’s Napoleon is less of a historical biopic and more of a awful fever dream where an artillery genius spends his free time blasting cannonballs at ancient pyramids for target practice, snagging front row VIP tickets to Marie Antoinette’s execution from 400 miles away, and recklessly leading cavalry charges with his sword raised like an angry French Braveheart. Throw in 49 year old Joaquin Phoenix playing a 24 year old lieutenant while his canonically older wife is portrayed by an actress 14 years his junior, and it becomes clear the script treated actual history as a vague, polite suggestion. It's a goofy ass visual spectacle. 

"You think you're so great because you have boats!"

Hard to say about Lee, The Crow 1994 is an cult classic.  Maybe he would have fought for top action roles with Keanu Reeves.  Dude was cool.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Giancarlo Esposito playing Vernon Dahmer in By Any Means feels like an interesting break from his recent roles

**Score:** 25
**Body:** Giancarlo Esposito has become so associated with calm and intimidating authority figures that I almost expect him to be the antagonist whenever he appears.

In By Any Means he’s playing Vernon Dahmer instead. Dahmer was a real civil rights leader in Mississippi who helped Black residents register to vote and was murdered after the KKK attacked his home in 1966.

It feels like a much different use of Esposito than Gus Fring, Stan Edgar or Moff Gideon. I want to know whether roles like this will remind people how much range he actually has beyond the controlled villain characters he’s become known for.

What do you guys think of the casting?

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Good for him! He had a supporting role in a Netflix series The Residence (pretty good detective show). In it his character has some sensitivity and a little dry humor that made me want to see him as a romantic lead. I believe he is on the record saying he would like to have the chance to do a romcom and lighter roles.
  - Would be cool to see him get more roles where he can actually be funny and charming for once.

## 2. Digital restorations are great, but they always go too far in removing every blemish and artifact

**Score:** 20
**Body:** When you watch a movie on film, it will always have a few artifacts and blemishes on it.  That's the nature of the physical medium.  I've seen movies on film both when it was the standard mode of presentation and for more modern special screenings, and while the movie always looks great, there are definitely times when you see some specks of dust on the film.  That's just how it goes.

At home, people try to replicate the cinema as much as possible.  People buy 4Ks of movies because they're supposedly as close to film as you can get digitally.  We love to see film grain in our old movies!  But whenever a film is digitally restored, they remove evey single blemish from the print.  That's just not a realistic digital recreation of a film.  You would never see the movie on film and have it be so perfect.

I'm not saying restorers shouldn't remove \*any\* blemishes; it's still important to clean up these old prints.  But we should leave a few intact to celebrate the way the film actually looked in theaters, not clean everything up just because we can.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. There's a world of difference between the beautiful work that Criterion and BFI do, for example, compared to the recent abominations from James Cameron, though. 

I don't need cigarette burns and bad splices when the film's grain, texture and contrast is preserved and restored. But I'd take anything over scrubbed prints where all the texture and grain and skin pores have been reduced to a silly putty type gloss!
2. The goal isn't to replicate the cinema, the goal is to replicate the original intent of the film. Dust, dirt, and scratches are extraneous intrusions onto the film (unless you're talking about something like "Grindhouse" or the newsreel portion of "Citizen Kane," where they are SUPPOSED to look distressed).

Film grain should be preserved, as it is part of the film itself.
3. *they remove evey single blemish from the print. That's just not a realistic digital recreation of a film. You would never see the movie on film and have it be so perfect.*

Of course you would. That’s how they look before age and use degrade 
them. 

There’s a point to be made about over smoothing and turning people into wax looking figures.

But this isn’t that. 

Stick to groceries for now 
4. Archival quality prints generally don't have those blemishes. Old beater prints do.

If you watched a film at its premier you would see a pristine print. Not sure why you want to replicate damage.
5. Film grain and blemishes aren't the same. Grain is just the nature of the medium. It's like the texture of a canvas. Blemishes like dirt or scratches have nothing to do with that, no relation to the original artistic intention or the original theater experience.
6. That very much depends on the institution and the people who are attached to the restauration. There is no such thing as a consensus across institutions but generally speaking, those who are state funded and less dependent on making profits are more likely to keep imperfections. This text by the Fiaf on Image Restoration, Manipulation, Treatment, and Ethics might be interesting to read for you: 
https://www.fiafnet.org/pages/E-Resources/Digital-Statement-part-III.html
7. It varies and I haven't followed it closely enough to see why some smooth out film grain and others don't. I suspect that the preservationists who don't smooth out film grain are purists and are backed by filmmakers (Scorsese, etc.) who prioritize the original look of these films. The ones who don't I think are prioritizing the look when it is streamed, which don't handle grain as well as it often seen as artifacts.
8. The team that did the digital restoration of the original STAR TREK deserves an award. There is a whole long story about that, but they created absolutely amazing work and put in an unbelievable amount of time and care. In fact, the process was so complicated and so time-consuming that it sort of put off some other restorations.

Sort of a curious thing about blemishes, though: Sometimes the restoration is restoring something that wasn't meant to be seen in the first place. I’m thinking of THE TWILIGHT ZONE episode “EYE OF THE BEHOLDER” (November 11, 1960). As I understand it, they used the original 35 mm film elements, which created some problems by revealing things that, if you were watching it on a small 1960 black-and-white television screen, you weren’t meant to see. The Blu-ray is wonderful, but it’s a bit of a spoiler.
9. Check out Bait (2019) if you have a fetish for artifacts. Shot on 16 mm with hand wound cameras and processed by hand. Very unusual looking. Good movie too.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rWPi3CZLnfU

## 3. Sight & Sound 250 Countdown Video

**Score:** 6
**Body:** I thought this would be the best place to share this title card supercut of Sight & Sound's top 250 from 2022. 

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fLzSpgsLCh8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fLzSpgsLCh8)

With a bit more time over the summer, I dove back into the list from four years back to watch some films still unseen. I was inspired to make this after thinking about how distinct each title card was for a given film. It was great fun to make, and I hope is objectively of interest so as not be blatant self-promotion. 

Tracking down the films was a pain, but locating the cards themselves was interesting. Here are some tidbits on what I found out:

Unsurprisingly, most title cards appear very early in the film’s runtime, usually within the first minute. Pre-1970s films are the best bets, sticking to a pretty standard formula: after the production logo, and perhaps the names of the director/leading actors, it’ll appear less than a minute in.  
  
Other films display their title card after (or during) a brief prologue scene, like in *Battle of Algiers* (3 minutes in) or *Yi Yi* (4 minutes in). There are countless others.   
  
Some films take longer: *Come and See* takes nearly 7 minutes, *Tropical Malady* 9 minutes. The credits for Kiarostami’s *Close-Up* do not start until nearly 16 minutes in.   
  
A few films wait the entire length of the film: *Moonlight* holds off on showing its title card until after the last shot, as does *Touch of Evil.* The title and end credits overlay the final shot of *Once Upon a Time in the West.*   
  
All of these are still pretty easy to track down. A few films make things more challenging.  
  
Two films are missing proper title cards: *Apocalypse Now* and *Portrait of a Lady on Fire.* *Portrait of a Lady on Fire* only displays its title in the closing credits, so I used that here. Most versions of *Apocalypse Now* have no credits whatsoever, just a copyright notice in its closing shot. I used the end credit sequence that Coppola has apparently discarded in most rereleased versions of the film.   
  
*Distant Voices* is best known as *Distant Voices, Still Lives.* The film is split into two parts with two seperate title cards: *Distant Voices* appears at the start, while *Still Lives* appears halfway through the film. I chose to only use the first.   
  
And finally, blink and you missed it: the title card for *Wavelength* is only about six frames (1/4 of a second) long.



Because of the issue with ties, I figured using a ranked list would be easiest, so I based it off of this one [https://letterboxd.com/sightsoundmag/list/sight-and-sounds-greatest-films-of-all-time/](https://letterboxd.com/sightsoundmag/list/sight-and-sounds-greatest-films-of-all-time/)

Of course, simply watching might inspire old debates from four years back. I more enjoy the selection of films, rather than care too much about the order, what's undeservingly included, and what has been left out. I think it's best to take the S&S list as merely a sample that is useful for exploring the canon.

  




### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. There are some very suspect films on this list, but when is that no the case. It's interesting how few films from recent years make the list. The one from 2012 was better. I liked seeing Star Wars ahead of Annie Hall. Kubrick along with a few other directors are overlooked. 

I won't get into the controversy over the #1 choice. I actually kind of prefer that spot not being solidified. There was clearly too much bias involved with the 2022 poll though unfortunately.

Anyway, excellent idea and work with the title cards.
  - Jeanne Dielman gonna be paying you a house call for this slander 🔪
    - Hahaha. Jeanne Myers.
2. This is really interesting. I love creative usage of a title card. My personal favorite is the usage in Climax, marking the end of Act 1, a major tonal shift, and a transition into a (perceived) extended oner all at once.

## 4. A Stomach Knot of a Movie- Images (1972)

**Score:** 6
**Body:** 

Note: It has spoilers. This post is for discussion on IMAGES (1972); if you intend to watch (I 'fiercely' recommended) probably come back later & make this discussion enriching. Additionally, I've not used AI to write /refine this, so please pardon grammatical errors! 

So, I'm on a horror movie spree! & This is the 3rd one I've watched! (Shining, Posession & this one). 

Just finished watching Images (1972)! Oh! What an amazing movie! It's a sort of movie which sustains a contortion in your stomach all through. You just get an eerie vibe. It's like something wrong is happening or you even start feeling a little dizzy because of the fractured sense of perception. At some points it's like WTF IS HAPPENING? The protagonist's (the main lady's) countenance is super amazing all through. Her perplexed expressions & the ever-changing face (adapting) stirs multiple emotions & she is able to convey the fractured sense of perception which she is feeling. Also, the director quite beautifully dropped the cue towards the end- when the imagined lover's kid said that she'd conjure up (wholly a mental construct) a friend if she felt lonely. I believe the protagonist lady did exactly the same thing. It also was indicative of her troubled childhood. She is the striking example of how fucked up things can get. It's like towards the end you simply can't discern satisfactorily as to what really transpired & what was figment of her imagination except the fact that her partner was dead. Also, the scenic beauty of the location where the film was shot was simply breathtaking. It unknowingly renders a sense of contrast to the central theme of the film (Super tensed). 

Also, may god bless each one of us with a partner like hers. If you're an atheist, then I'd say I wish the universe gives us an opportunity to experience this sort of companionship. He was so tolerant to such an imprudent & super unstable partner. 

Superb. Thanks to the individual who suggested this to me in one of my recommendation solicitation post! I'd be watching other movies too. HONESTLY, No AI search gave me this gem. AI simply can't replace reddit! 

What's your take on the movie? 

### Top 0 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)


## 5. Who are the most IMPORTANT Directors that have Influenced Cinema the most?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Been thinking about the directors that have impacted cinema the most and have influenced the most filmmakers that have followed them and why. These are the directors that I thought of, so far. 



Akira Kurosawa - mainly Seven Samurai, which formed and perfected the template in how you execute an ensemble film

  
Alfred Hitchcock - Template for the thriller and how to structure it in terms of pacing. You can see the huge influence he had on Chris Nolan.

  
Stanley Kubrick - Mainly 2001: A Space Odyssey (a film i don't like). The use of cutting edge special effects and the first truly dynamic and well-made science-fiction film, which influenced every director going into that genre

  
Ridley Scott - Lighting and how to use it to effectively depict a world. Mainly Blade Runner which i think is the film that has the best lighting in any film. Pretty much every film that does a world in the future uses his aesthetic and lighting technique. 

  
Any directors I am missing, feel free to add.

7. Your four seem to be directors only within a very limited timeframe and set of genres. Of course Kurosawa, Hitchcock, and Kubrick are big names that a lot of passionate cinema fans love, and for good reason. I don't think Ridley Scott deserves as high of praise, though you're right that he did raise the bar on visual elements of filmmaking for his time, especially early on.

There are whole history-of-cinema books that could add several dozen directors to your list, especially in the earlier eras. Georges Melies, Cecil B. Demille, D.W. Griffith, Sergei Eistenstein, Buster Keaton, Charlie Chaplin, F.W. Murnau, Orson Welles and others had major influences early on.

Then you have big names like John Ford, Howard Hawks, Ernst Lubitsch, Preston Sturges, Billy Wilder, George Cukor, Frank Capra, Vincente Minelli, Victor Fleming, Douglas Sirk and others whose filmmaking style defined most of what we consider the modern movie.

Then by the 1950-60s (and before that too) you had a whole "new wave" of directors, many of them coming from or influenced by other countries, including Ingmar Bergman, Federico Fellini, Jean Cocteau, Jean-Luc Godard, Samuel Fuller, Sam Peckinpah, Sergio Leone, Francois Truffaut, Michael Powell, Otto Preminger, Blake Edwards, and probably 40 other names I should mention.

If you're going to talk about the 1970s then you have to start mentioning the new names in Hollywood that include young upstarts like Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. Or Francis Coppola, Brian DePalma, Mike Nichols, Don Siegel, Arthur Penn, John Schlesinger, Sidney Lumet, Robert Altman, James Bridges, Sydney Pollack, Alan J. Pakula, and dozens of other names. You'd also have to mention the massive influence of Disney in affecting the entire landscape of children's and family movies.

If you're just talking about "influence" then obviously some names are bigger than others, and Hitchcock, Kurosawa, and Kubrick are good choices but they couldn't have done any of it without their peers and forebears.

I'm probably missing/dissing a hundred noteworthy names here, including lots of foreign directors (plenty of other excellent Japanese directors besides Kurosawa), indie filmmakers, experimentalists (Stan Brakhage) and those with less commercial appeal or success. I also am hesitant to mention the influence of Woody Allen, because his name is mud, but the more conversational and personal style of romantic-comedy or quirky-comedy that became a big deal in the 1990s through 2010s was to an extent forged by him, though of course not exclusively.

Once you start talking about the 1980s and 1990s, there are even more names that should be thrown into the mix. I won't even try because this will be 2x longer as a post.

It's also not right to discount the influence of radio, the theater scene, and the rise of TV and video-rental when discussing the ways film style and subject matter have shifted over time. Or the way that the post-WWII baby boom affected which films get made and what subject matter was emphasized (and received financing) from one decade to another.
